kartellrecht-all.title: Antitrust law: cartel prohibition, fines, and personal liability
kartellrecht-all.description: Six lessons on competition law at work: from the basics of the cartel prohibition and market dominance, through hardcore restrictions and risk scenarios, the fine framework and the role of compliance programs, self-cleaning under procurement law, to individual criminal liability for bid-rigging – closing with a checkpoint on where fines turn into personal liability.

kartellrecht-l0.title: The cartel prohibition: agreements, market power, and price control

kartellrecht-l0-s1.title: Three forms of conduct, one shared test: object or effect
kartellrecht-l0-s1.body: Sec. 1 GWB prohibits three forms of conduct: agreements between undertakings, decisions by associations of undertakings, and concerted practices – almost identical in wording to Art. 101(1) TFEU. What matters is the "object or effect" test: the anticompetitive object alone is enough, an actual harmful effect on the market does not have to be proven. For so-called hardcore restrictions – price-fixing, market or customer allocation, for example – this means a market-analysis defense ("but there was no actual effect") does not apply: the anticompetitive object alone already establishes the violation. The concept of a "concerted practice" is also deliberately broad and requires no explicit agreement: if a sales director informally discusses future price-increase plans with a competitor at an industry event, that can already satisfy the offense – even without specific figures being mentioned or a formal resolution being reached. This is exactly why trade-association meetings are treated as a classic risk scenario in competition law: mere attendance is not the problem, the content of what gets discussed on the sidelines is.

kartellrecht-l0-s2.title: Holding market dominance is legal – abusing it is not
kartellrecht-l0-s2.body: Sec. 18(4) GWB presumes an undertaking to be dominant once its market share reaches at least 40 percent – a rebuttable presumption, not an automatic violation. What follows from that position is governed by a different provision: Sec. 19(1) GWB does not prohibit the dominant position itself, only its abuse – market leadership earned through superior performance remains entirely lawful. Sec. 19(2) GWB gives standard examples: exclusionary abuse (unfairly impeding or, without objective justification, treating other undertakings differently) and exploitative abuse (demanding prices or terms that deviate from those that would result under effective competition). Sec. 19 GWB thus mirrors Art. 102 TFEU and targets unilateral conduct by a single undertaking – unlike Sec. 1 GWB, no agreement between several undertakings is required. A third, often underestimated trap sits between market levels: if a manufacturer contractually dictates fixed or minimum resale prices to its dealers ("resale price maintenance"), that is a hardcore restriction under Art. 4(a) of the Vertical Block Exemption Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2022/720) – regardless of the fact that manufacturer and dealer are not competitors at all. Only non-binding recommended prices and maximum prices remain permissible, and only as long as they do not, through supply-cutoff threats or incentives, effectively function as fixed or minimum prices.

kartellrecht-l1.title: Hardcore restrictions in practice: from price-fixing to the dawn raid

kartellrecht-l1-s1.title: What a hardcore restriction is – and, notably, what it is not
kartellrecht-l1-s1.body: Hardcore restrictions are the top tier of competition-law violations: price-fixing between competitors, allocating customers or territories, and coordinated bids in public tenders (bid-rigging) are all uncontroversially treated as such. Not covered, by contrast, is an undertaking's unilateral internal decision to lower its own prices – that simply lacks the necessary two-undertaking element of Sec. 1 GWB, and is ordinary competition. Two recent EU cases show how broad the spectrum of real-world cases has become: in June 2025 the EU Commission fined Delivery Hero and Glovo EUR 329 million – its first-ever decision on a pure labour-market cartel ("no-poach"): the two companies agreed not to poach each other's employees and additionally allocated national markets, even though Delivery Hero held only a minority stake in Glovo. In April 2025 the Commission fined 15 car manufacturers and the industry association ACEA EUR 458 million, because for more than 15 years they had agreed not to advertise their vehicles' recyclability and not to compete on end-of-life-vehicle recycling payments – a cartel over non-competition on environmental information rather than price. Both cases confirm: hardcore restrictions are not a theoretical edge case, and are long past being only classic price-fixing.

kartellrecht-l1-s2.title: Two preventive scenarios: the unannounced inspection and merger control
kartellrecht-l1-s2.body: Two preventive scenarios confront anyone dealing with competition law, regardless of the underlying violation. First, the unannounced inspection ("dawn raid"): under Sec. 59b GWB the competition authority may search business premises, and the EU Commission has corresponding powers under Art. 20 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2003 – entering premises, examining and copying records, sealing premises and documents. The right response is to cooperate: submit to the inspection, destroy nothing, open nothing that has been sealed, and inform the legal department and external counsel immediately. Counsel may be called in, but inspectors are not required to wait indefinitely for their arrival – obstruction is punished separately: under Art. 23(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1/2003, fines of up to 1 percent of total turnover apply; in 2008 the Commission fined E.ON EUR 38 million for a single broken seal alone. Second, merger control – a standalone preventive regime alongside the cartel prohibition: if a merger exceeds the EUMR's turnover thresholds (Regulation (EC) No 139/2004, in the primary case EUR 5 billion combined worldwide turnover and EUR 250 million EU-wide turnover for at least two parties), it must be notified before implementation and may only be completed after clearance (Art. 4, 7 EUMR). The difference from the cartel prohibition: merger control reviews a lasting structural change in advance, while the cartel prohibition sanctions coordination between undertakings that remain legally independent.

kartellrecht-l2.title: Fines: caps, the compliance bonus, and damages exposure

kartellrecht-l2-s1.title: 10 percent of group turnover as the cap – and what lowers the fine within that ceiling
kartellrecht-l2-s1.body: The fine cap under Sec. 81c(2) GWB stands at 10 percent of the total turnover achieved in the preceding business year – and specifically the worldwide turnover of the entire economic unit (corporate group), not just the individual participating legal entity (Sec. 81c(5) GWB). For less serious, mostly procedural violations, Abs. 3 sets a lower 1 percent cap. Within that ceiling, Sec. 81d GWB governs how the specific fine amount is assessed: appropriate and effective precautions to prevent and detect violations – taken both before and after the offense – can be considered as a mitigating factor. This is a mitigation, not a guarantee: if the violation was orchestrated by company management itself, it effectively does not apply. What makes a compliance program effective, the Bundeskartellamt has clarified itself: it explicitly rejects mechanically ticking off as many measures as possible, requiring instead a program tailored to the undertaking's size, organization, and risk. It names nine flexible, non-mandatory building blocks – including risk analysis, tone from the top, staff training and selection, whistleblower systems – but prescribes neither a specific training frequency nor a fixed review interval. That sets competition-law compliance clearly apart from anti-money-laundering law, where Sec. 6(2) No. 6 GwG imposes an explicit, ongoing training duty.

kartellrecht-l2-s2.title: When code words come to light: the road-construction case – and what still looms afterward
kartellrecht-l2-s2.body: How a hardcore restriction gets disguised in practice is shown by the August 2026 road-construction case: the Bundeskartellamt fined six companies EUR 60.3 million for years of customer allocation and bid-rigging. The participants met monthly in Kassel and communicated their coordination by phone, email, or messenger using coded terms – mileage readings, beer or sausage prices, sponsorship amounts, hotel room rates – as cover for actual bid figures. Alongside the corporate fine under Sec. 1 GWB, the public prosecutor's office is separately investigating individuals involved for possible bid-rigging under Sec. 298 StGB. Paying the fine, moreover, often does not end a case like this for the companies involved: under Sec. 33a(1) GWB, cartel participants must compensate injured parties for the damage caused, and Sec. 33a(2) GWB rebuttably presumes that a cartel causes damage at all – so claimants do not have to prove the occurrence of harm from scratch. Under Sec. 33b GWB, the civil court is additionally bound by the competition authority's final infringement finding, so "follow-on" claims do not need to re-establish the violation itself. An important exception applies to a leniency applicant with full fine immunity: under Sec. 33e GWB, it is in principle liable only to its own direct and indirect customers and suppliers. Cartel damages can substantially exceed the fine itself, making them a standalone compliance argument, not just a footnote to the fine.

kartellrecht-l3.title: Self-cleaning under Sec. 125 GWB: regaining tender eligibility

kartellrecht-l3-s1.title: Three cumulative requirements, none sufficient on its own
kartellrecht-l3-s1.body: An undertaking that would otherwise have to be excluded from public tender procedures because of a competition-law violation can regain its eligibility through successful "self-cleaning." Sec. 125(1) GWB requires three cumulative conditions, none of which is sufficient on its own: first, compensation for any damage caused by the offense (or a corresponding commitment to pay); second, comprehensive clarification of the facts and circumstances through active cooperation with the investigating authorities; and third, concrete technical, organizational, and personnel measures suitable to prevent further violations. Improved competition-law training is part of this third, combined requirement – the statutory text names the technical, organizational, and personnel aspects together as one unit, not as separately labeled categories – but it is not sufficient alone: compensation and clarification-cooperation must also be in place. If the contracting authority or the Bundeskartellamt considers the measures taken insufficient, it must, taking into account the severity and particular circumstances of the offense, give the undertaking the reasons for that decision (Sec. 125(2) GWB) – the statute prescribes no specific form for this, and in particular no written-form requirement.

kartellrecht-l3-s2.title: What self-cleaning does NOT cure – and its EU-wide foundation
kartellrecht-l3-s2.body: Self-cleaning specifically cures only one problem: an impending exclusion from public tender procedures. A fine already imposed as final remains unaffected, and so does any individual criminal liability of persons involved under Sec. 298 StGB. On the precise nature of the exclusion risk: Sec. 123 GWB lists mandatory exclusion grounds, while Sec. 124 GWB lists facultative grounds left to the contracting authority's discretion – pure competition-law administrative offenses typically fall under the discretionary ground in Sec. 124 GWB, so exclusion is not automatically mandatory in every case. A second, practically important lever sits in the competition register (Wettbewerbsregister) at the Bundeskartellamt: entries based on fine decisions are deleted under Sec. 7 WRegG at the latest 3 years after the decision is issued, entries based on certain criminal convictions at the latest after 5 years; before that period expires, an undertaking can apply to the register authority under Sec. 8 WRegG for early deletion based on demonstrated self-cleaning. This entire framework is not purely a German invention: Art. 57(6) of EU Public Procurement Directive 2014/24/EU guarantees economic operators across the Union exactly these three routes to demonstrate reliability, and Art. 57(7) additionally caps the maximum exclusion period at 5 years for mandatory and 3 years for facultative exclusion grounds (implemented in Sec. 126 GWB). For internationally active undertakings, the self-cleaning logic therefore applies in every EU member state, not only in Germany.

kartellrecht-l4.title: Individual criminal liability: Sec. 298 StGB and the limits of leniency protection

kartellrecht-l4-s1.title: Up to five years' imprisonment – with a way back
kartellrecht-l4-s1.body: Sec. 298 StGB criminalizes submitting a tender offer based on an unlawful agreement – imprisonment of up to 5 years, or a fine (Abs. 1). Abs. 2 extends this liability to negotiated-award procedures preceded by a competitive selection process. This is individual criminal liability, in addition to the corporate fine under the GWB, and it targets exactly one hardcore restriction specifically: bid-rigging. Price-fixing or market allocation outside a tender procedure, by contrast, triggers no standalone criminal statute for individuals in Germany – an important, often underestimated distinction. Sec. 298(3) StGB contains a voluntary-withdrawal provision: a person remains exempt from punishment who voluntarily prevents the rigged offer's acceptance, or genuinely and seriously attempts to do so. The active-conduct requirement is decisive – mere internal regret without action does not suffice; a purely passive "I didn't mean it that way" protects no one from prosecution.

kartellrecht-l4-s2.title: The leniency program saves the company – not automatically the employees
kartellrecht-l4-s2.body: The leniency program (Bonusregelung, Secs. 81h ff. GWB) rewards undertakings that are first to disclose their cartel involvement and cooperate comprehensively with a fine reduction, up to and including full immunity. An undertaking that has not yet fully clarified the facts but wants to secure its place in line can first file a "marker" under Sec. 81m GWB: a declaration of willingness to cooperate containing a few minimum details, which secures its rank in the order of leniency applications. If the undertaking submits the fully worked-out application within the deadline set by the authority, the marker's timestamp counts – decisive, because the leniency program is a race: as a rule only the first applicant obtains full immunity, all later applicants only a reduction. In the road-construction case, four of the six companies obtained a fine reduction this way. What the leniency program does NOT do: it concerns exclusively the remission or reduction of fines in the administrative-offense proceedings against the company. Prosecution for bid-rigging under Sec. 298 StGB is a matter for the public prosecutor's office, which is bound by the mandatory-prosecution principle and over which the Bundeskartellamt has no disposal power – unlike, for example, the US leniency program, German law contains no formal, automatic immunity guarantee for the individuals involved. The company's leniency decision and the individual defense interests of the employees involved must therefore be assessed and advised on separately.

kartellrecht-l5.title: Hardcore restrictions and criminal offenses: where the fine chain turns into personal liability

kartellrecht-l5-s1.title: Not every hardcore restriction carries the same risk for individuals
kartellrecht-l5-s1.body: Not every hardcore restriction carries the same risk for individuals. Price-fixing, market or customer allocation, and output limitation remain, in Germany, administrative offenses for the companies involved under Sec. 1 GWB, sanctioned with fines of up to 10 percent of worldwide group turnover (Sec. 81c(2) GWB) – the individual who acted generally faces no standalone criminal statute of their own. Exactly one category breaks this pattern: bid-rigging. Anyone who submits a tender offer based on an unlawful agreement becomes personally criminally liable under Sec. 298 StGB – imprisonment of up to 5 years or a fine, independent of and in addition to the fine against the company. The reason for this break is not that bid-rigging is inherently more severe than the other hardcore restrictions, but that the legislature gave public tenders their own protected legal interest with a dedicated criminal statute – a protection that simply does not exist for pure price-fixing or market allocation outside procurement procedures in Germany. The road-construction case from the "Fines" chapter makes this dual character concrete: the very same customer allocation and bid manipulation triggered both a fine under Sec. 1 GWB against the six companies involved and a parallel investigation under Sec. 298 StGB against the individuals who acted – two separate proceedings, two separate levels of liability, one and the same underlying conduct.

kartellrecht-l5-s2.title: Two misconceptions, clearly corrected
kartellrecht-l5-s2.body: Two common misconceptions deserve a clear correction at this point. First: a company's successful leniency application (Secs. 81h ff. GWB) does not automatically protect the employees involved from prosecution under Sec. 298 StGB – in the road-construction case, four companies received a fine reduction, while the public prosecutor's office independently investigated individuals under Sec. 298 StGB. The leniency program concerns exclusively the administrative-offense proceedings against the company; prosecution is decided by the public prosecutor's office, which is bound by the mandatory-prosecution principle, and German law contains no formal individual immunity guarantee. Second: "cartel violations are just a matter of corporate fines everywhere" is a dangerous misconception internationally. Germany, with its model – administrative offense for companies, individual criminal liability only for bid-rigging – is the exception rather than the rule: in the US, a violation of Sec. 1 of the Sherman Act for price-fixing, market allocation, and bid-rigging is a felony, individuals face up to 10 years' imprisonment and fines of up to USD 1 million, and the Department of Justice actively prosecutes managers. In the United Kingdom, the "cartel offence" under s. 188 Enterprise Act 2002 criminalizes individual participation in price-fixing, market-sharing, output-limitation, and bid-rigging arrangements – up to 5 years' imprisonment. For employees with international business, personal criminal liability is therefore real, not just a German peculiarity – and that is exactly why this module closes with the message it opened with: the anticompetitive object alone establishes the violation, and at tenders, it can become deeply personal.
